questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to an academically strong university. Preferably in an English speaking country, in a place with history.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: All I needed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are student halls operated by the university.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Some halls are catered(with food) either 14 or 19 meals a week, or you can choose a self-catered hall where you will have to cook in the shared kitchens. There are also kitchens in the catered halls. The catered food is decent.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is a great way to meet people. Most students living in some of the halls are first years, so they will be 18-20. I think some of the newer self-catered halls, like David Russell Apartments or Fife park, have more students, who are not first years. They are also located a little further from the centre of town.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have to meet with an academic advisor and tell them the courses you want to take, they will then look up the schedules and prerequisites for the courses, and decide whether you can take them or not.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The advisors, you can also email professors asking for information about the modules.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had originally wanted to do 5000-level modules, but since I am an undergraduate student, they only let me take one of those two, which was already an exception, because undergraduate students are normally not allowed to do 5000-level modules.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look at the modules at home, and have backups in case some of them dont work out.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I think the level is comparable to KU. Some undergraduate mathematics courses at KU are classified graduate courses at St. Andrews, which means the level might be slightly higher at St. Andrews, but not a big difference. The workload is comparable, but slightly higher in the exam period compared to SCIENCE at KU at least.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Less assignments at St. Andrews. There are tutorials where you will discuss weekly exercises, and in these tutorials you will be more involved and discussing with the professor than at KU, especially if you do a module with less students.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MT5865 - Measure Theory
MT3504 - Differential Equations
CS3302 - Data Encoding
CS3105 - Artificial Intelligence

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
CS3105 is a nice intro to AI, but should be easy if you have taken the machine learning courses at KU.
CS3302 is interesting and well taught, and it is something you can't really do at KU.
The MT5865 professor is good.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not unexpected, but spent quite a bit at pubs, a pint is about £5.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Trains are more expensive than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are societies for everything. Go to the freshers fair and talk to the societies and go to some events, you can end up getting a lot of free food. There are also lots of sports clubs that are not too expensive. The athletic facilities are very good.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join some societies and/or sports clubs. Most students are involved in something and it is a great way to meet people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See St. Andrews. Go to the highland. See Edinburgh.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. There are a lot of internationals who all adjust quickly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Good luck, there are not many local students, most are from USA or England. But living in halls or joining a sport is an easy way to meet student at St. Andrews. Go out to a bunch of events in Freshers week.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing was really challenging.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Everybody was pretty open and nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Experience some of the rest of Scotland. Join societies or clubs. Enjoy what St. Andrews has to offer, but dont forget to study, the exams are not all easy.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing a different culture and meeting people from lots of different places. Trying a different way of studying compared to KU.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being away from Denmark, and having to meet new people all the time.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
